title: Spectral Analysis of Signals — shard 2: Chapters 3–4

The PDF retains Prentice Hall copyright and states all rights reserved; no redistribution or adaptation permission is asserted.
topics: 3.1 Introduction (printed pp. 86–87) — model-based spectral estimation, rational versus discrete spectra, model-order selection, and the role of consistency and Cramér–Rao limits.
3.2 Signals with Rational Spectra (pp. 87–88) — rational PSDs, spectral factorization, stable/minimum-phase ARMA representations, and AR/MA/ARMA naming conventions.
3.3 Covariance Structure of ARMA Processes (pp. 88–90) — covariance recurrences induced by A(z)y(t)=B(z)e(t).
3.4 AR Signals (pp. 90–94) — all-pole modeling of narrow peaks and linear parameter estimation.
3.4.1 Yule–Walker Method (pp. 90–91) — Toeplitz normal equations, biased sample covariances, AR coefficients, and innovation variance.
3.4.2 Least Squares Method (pp. 91–94) — linear prediction, finite-sample regression, autocorrelation versus covariance LS variants, stability and accuracy tradeoffs.
3.5 Order–Recursive Solutions to the Yule–Walker Equations (pp. 94–101) — exploitation of Hermitian Toeplitz structure across candidate orders.
3.5.1 Levinson–Durbin Algorithm (pp. 96–97) — reflection coefficients, order recursion, prediction-error variance, and O(n_max²) complexity.
3.5.2 Delsarte–Genin Algorithm (pp. 97–101) — split-Levinson recursion for real-valued covariance sequences using symmetric vectors.
3.6 MA Signals (pp. 101–103) — broad peaks and sharp nulls, nonlinear MA parameter estimation, finite covariance support, and the Blackman–Tukey connection.
3.7 ARMA Signals (pp. 103–109) — pole-zero models for simultaneous peaks and nulls and the lack of a universally satisfactory estimator.
3.7.1 Modified Yule–Walker Method (pp. 103–106) — overdetermined covariance equations, LS/TLS solutions, weighting, conditioning, and MA covariance recovery.
3.7.2 Two–Stage Least Squares Method (pp. 106–109) — high-order AR whitening followed by ARMA regression; bias/order tradeoff and Durbin’s MA method.
3.8 Multivariate ARMA Signals (pp. 109–117) — representation nonuniqueness, canonical parameterizations, and multichannel subspace estimation.
3.8.1 ARMA State–Space Equations (pp. 109–113) — shaping filters, covariance matrices, Riccati reconstruction, similarity transformations, and minimality.
3.8.2 Subspace Parameter Estimation — Theoretical Aspects (pp. 113–114) — block-Hankel covariance factorization, rank/model order, SVD, and shift invariance.
3.8.3 Subspace Parameter Estimation — Implementation Aspects (pp. 114–117) — normalized future/past data, practical rank, LS/TLS recovery, Riccati failure fallback.
3.9 Complements (pp. 117–129) — deeper results supporting prediction, covariance extension, structured inversion, and MA fitting.
3.9.1 Partial Autocorrelation Sequence (pp. 117–118) — reflection coefficients as normalized residual correlation after intermediate samples are removed.
3.9.2 Properties of Covariance Extensions (pp. 118–119) — admissible-disk construction, infinite extensions, and maximum-entropy AR completion.
3.9.3 Burg Method for AR Parameter Estimation (pp. 119–122) — joint forward/backward prediction-error recursion and guaranteed stability.
3.9.4 Gohberg–Semencul Formula (pp. 122–125) — structured closed form for the inverse of a Hermitian Toeplitz covariance matrix.
3.9.5 MA Parameter Estimation in Polynomial Time (pp. 125–129) — nearest nonnegative MA spectrum, covariance fitting, semidefinite parameterization, and interior-point solution.
3.10 Exercises (pp. 129–143) — proofs, predictor/smoother identities, stability, model comparison, Monte Carlo super-resolution, order selection, and sunspot/lynx measured-data studies.
4.1 Introduction (pp. 144–148) — complex sinusoids in white noise, random phases, line spectra, parameter identifiability, and high-resolution frequency estimation.
4.2 Models of Sinusoidal Signals in Noise (pp. 148–151) — three equivalent-purpose descriptions retaining frequency information.
4.2.1 Nonlinear Regression Model (pp. 148–149) — direct sinusoidal samples with frequency as a nonlinear parameter.
4.2.2 ARMA Model (p. 149) — unit-circle annihilating filter and degenerate pole-zero description.
4.2.3 Covariance Matrix Model (pp. 149–151) — Vandermonde steering matrix, low-rank signal covariance plus white-noise floor, and lagged block covariance.
4.3 Nonlinear Least Squares Method (pp. 151–155) — concentrated likelihood, Cramér–Rao efficiency, colored-noise robustness, multimodal optimization, and periodogram relation.
4.4 High–Order Yule–Walker Method (pp. 155–159) — high-order annihilation, rank-truncated SVD covariance equations, LS/TLS recovery, and root selection.
4.5 Pisarenko and MUSIC Methods (pp. 159–164) — signal/noise eigenspaces, spectral and root MUSIC, pseudospectra, rank choice, and spurious-root control.
4.6 Min–Norm Method (pp. 164–166) — minimum-norm noise-subspace vector and spectral/root estimators.
4.7 ESPRIT Method (pp. 166–168) — rotational invariance of shifted Vandermonde subarrays and frequency recovery from eigenvalue phases.
4.8 Forward–Backward Approach (pp. 168–170) — persymmetric covariance averaging, finite-sample accuracy, conditioning, and why full Toeplitzization can be harmful.
4.9.1 Mean Square Convergence of Sample Covariances for Line Spectral Processes (pp. 170–172) — second-order ergodicity underlying covariance-based consistency.
4.9.2 Carathéodory Parameterization of a Covariance Matrix (pp. 172–174) — decomposition of any positive Toeplitz covariance into finitely many spectral lines plus white noise.
4.9.3 Unwindowed Periodogram for Sine-Wave Detection in White Noise (pp. 174–177) — chi-square peak statistics and a false-alarm-controlled detector.
4.9.4 NLS Frequency Estimation for a Sinusoidal Signal with Time-Varying Amplitude (pp. 177–179) — squaring demodulates an arbitrary real envelope and enables FFT estimation.
4.9.5 Monotonically Descending Techniques for Function Minimization (pp. 179–185) — cyclic minimization, majorization, RELAX, and expectation-maximization.
4.9.6 Frequency-Selective ESPRIT-Based Method (pp. 185–193) — FFT-band projection, interference suppression, reduced-rank SVD, and band-limited ESPRIT.
4.9.7 A Useful Result for Two-Dimensional Sinusoidal Signals (pp. 193–198) — linearly parameterized null-space bases for 2D damped or undamped sinusoids.
4.10 Exercises (pp. 198–206) — Doppler radar, ergodicity counterexamples, colored-noise variants, estimator equivalences, Monte Carlo resolution, order selection, and measured data.
Boundary note — this shard ends at printed p. 206; Chapters 5–6 and all appendices were not read or summarized.
key_results: §3.2, eqs. (3.2.1)–(3.2.4): rational PSDs are dense among continuous spectra and admit spectral factorization φ(ω)=σ²|B(ω)/A(ω)|², with reciprocal-conjugate pole/zero symmetry.
§3.2, eqs. (3.2.5)–(3.2.8): every rational PSD can be realized by filtering white noise through B(z)/A(z); AR, MA, and ARMA are the all-pole, all-zero, and pole-zero specializations.
§3.3, eq. (3.3.4): every ARMA(n,m) covariance sequence obeys r(k)+Σ_{i=1}^n a_i r(k-i)=0 for k>m, the recurrence behind covariance-based AR estimation.
§3.4.1, eqs. (3.4.2)–(3.4.5): the Yule–Walker solution is θ=−R_n^{-1}r_n, and σ² follows from the zero-lag equation; biased sample covariances preserve positive definiteness for any nonzero sample.
§3.4.2, eqs. (3.4.8)–(3.4.10): Yule–Walker is exactly the best linear-prediction solution, with minimum error variance σ_n²=r(0)−r_n*R_n^{-1}r_n.
§3.4.2, eqs. (3.4.11)–(3.4.13): covariance LS minimizes ||y+Yθ||² and gives θ̂=−(Y*Y)^{-1}Y*y; the autocorrelation LS choice is equivalent to Yule–Walker.
§3.4.2: Yule–Walker guarantees a stable estimated AR model, whereas covariance LS may rarely be unstable but is often more accurate at short or medium sample lengths.
§3.5.1, eqs. (3.5.7), (3.5.10), and (3.5.11): Levinson–Durbin updates the order through reflection coefficient k_{n+1}, θ_{n+1}=[θ_n;0]+k_{n+1}[θ̃_n;1], and σ_{n+1}²=σ_n²(1−|k_{n+1}|²).
§3.5.1: Levinson–Durbin obtains all orders through n_max in O(n_max²) work, versus O(n_max⁴) when independent general solves are used for every order.
§3.5.2: Delsarte–Genin exploits real-valued symmetry and is about twice as fast as Levinson–Durbin for real data.

§3.6, eqs. (3.6.2)–(3.6.4): an MA(m) process has r(k)=0 for |k|>m, making its direct covariance PSD estimate identical to a length-(2m+1) rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimate; it can be negative.

§3.7.1, eqs. (3.7.1)–(3.7.4): modified Yule–Walker estimates ARMA poles from lags beyond m; overdetermining the system can help narrowband cases when higher-lag covariance signal exceeds estimation noise.
§3.7.1: statistical and numerical accuracy track the condition number of the covariance regression; increasing M is useful only while the added lags improve conditioning and information.
§3.7.1, eqs. (3.7.7)–(3.7.9): after estimating A, the MA covariance polynomial is recovered by filtering the covariance through A; the resulting numerator is not guaranteed nonnegative.

§3.7.2, eqs. (3.7.15)–(3.7.16): two-stage LS first approximates the minimum-phase ARMA process by a high-order AR innovation filter, then regresses on estimated innovations; its PSD is positive by construction.
§3.7.2: the truncation order K controls a bias–variance tradeoff, and zeros near the unit circle require large K, making this a hard case for all ARMA estimators.
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.5)–(3.8.6): the multivariate state-space shaping filter is H(z)=z^{-1}C(I−Az^{-1})^{-1}B+I and its spectral density matrix is H(ω)QH*(ω).
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.13)–(3.8.19): positive-lag covariances factor as R_k=CA^{k−1}D; P, Q, and B follow from a Riccati equation and algebraic reconstruction.
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.20)–(3.8.25): state similarity makes fully parameterized (A,B,C) nonunique; minimality is equivalent to full rank of both observability-like and controllability-like matrices.
§3.8.2, eqs. (3.8.26)–(3.8.31): the block-Hankel covariance matrix factors as R=OC*, has rank n, and its SVD identifies state dimension and subspaces up to a nonsingular transform.

§3.8.3, eqs. (3.8.43)–(3.8.49): practical subspace estimation whitens future/past covariance blocks, chooses model order by the singular-value gap, uses LS/TLS shift fitting for A, and reconstructs P,Q,B.
§3.9.1, eq. (3.9.1): a Levinson reflection coefficient is the negative normalized correlation between forward and backward prediction residuals after intermediate samples have been projected out.

§3.9.2, eqs. (3.9.5)–(3.9.8): admissible next covariance values form an open disk; choosing each disk center sets all subsequent reflection coefficients to zero and yields the maximum-entropy AR extension.
§3.9.3, eqs. (3.9.11)–(3.9.16): Burg recursively minimizes the mean forward/backward error, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives |k̂_p|≤1, hence a stable AR estimate.

§3.9.4, eqs. (3.9.17)–(3.9.22): the Gohberg–Semencul displacement formula determines the entire inverse covariance matrix from the first inverse column despite the inverse generally not being Toeplitz.

§3.9.5, eqs. (3.9.25)–(3.9.31): an invalid negative MA estimate can be projected onto the cone of nonnegative trigonometric polynomials via covariance fitting and a semidefinite quadratic program solvable in polynomial time.
§4.1, eqs. (4.1.6)–(4.1.7): independent uniform phases give r(k)=Σα_p²e^{iω_pk}+σ²δ_{k,0} and φ(ω)=2πΣα_p²δ(ω−ω_p)+σ².

§4.1: high-resolution methods can resolve frequency separations below 1/N cycles/sample because they exploit the exact sinusoidal model, not because the classical Fourier resolution limit is violated without assumptions.

§4.2.2, eqs. (4.2.1)–(4.2.3): A(z)=∏(1−e^{iω_k}z^{-1}) annihilates the noise-free sinusoidal signal; its unit-circle roots encode all frequencies and cannot be canceled from the degenerate ARMA equation.
§4.2.3, eqs. (4.2.5)–(4.2.7): with m≥n and distinct frequencies, the Vandermonde matrix has rank n and R=APA*+σ²I separates a rank-n signal covariance from isotropic noise.
§4.3, eq. (4.3.8): concentrating NLS over complex amplitudes reduces frequency estimation to maximizing Y*B(B*B)^{-1}B*Y, after which amplitudes follow by ordinary LS.
§4.3, eq. (4.3.9): asymptotically Cov(ω̂)=6σ²N^{-3}diag(1/α_k²); under Gaussian white noise this reaches the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
§4.3: NLS remains consistent and asymptotically efficient under unknown colored Gaussian noise when SNR is interpreted locally as α_k²/φ_n(ω_k), unlike the subspace methods.

§4.3, eqs. (4.3.10)–(4.3.17): for one complex sinusoid, the NLS frequency is exactly the largest unwindowed-periodogram peak; for separated multiple lines, the n largest peaks give O(1/N) initial approximations.

§4.4, eqs. (4.4.10)–(4.4.16): the theoretical HOYW covariance matrix has rank n while its sample estimate is full rank; truncating the SVD to rank n both conditions and denoises the estimating equation.
§4.4: increasing L and M supplies more independent low-rank relations but makes higher-lag covariances less reliable and introduces possible spurious noise roots; L+M≈N/3 is suggested.
§4.5, eqs. (4.5.3)–(4.5.13): the smallest m−n eigenvalues equal σ², their eigenvectors span the noise subspace N(A*), and the true frequencies are the only zeros of a*(ω)GG*a(ω).
§4.5, eqs. (4.5.15)–(4.5.18): spectral MUSIC locates pseudospectrum peaks, root MUSIC selects reciprocal roots nearest the unit circle, and Pisarenko is MUSIC with m=n+1.

§4.6, eqs. (4.6.1)–(4.6.14): Min–Norm replaces the full MUSIC noise projector with the unique first-entry-normalized minimum-norm vector in the estimated noise subspace, retaining similar accuracy at lower cost.

§4.7, eqs. (4.7.3)–(4.7.12): deleting the first versus last Vandermonde row gives A_2=A_1D; the eigenvalues of the corresponding signal-subspace LS/TLS map are e^{-iω_k}, yielding ESPRIT frequencies without root sorting.
§4.8, eqs. (4.8.3)–(4.8.14): forward–backward averaging R̃=(R̂+JR̂^TJ)/2 enforces the true covariance’s persymmetry and usually improves short-sample estimation by using more lag products.

§4.8: full Toeplitz averaging is not automatically superior—at finite N and infinite SNR, forward or forward–backward matrices preserve rank n and exact frequencies, while Toeplitz averaging is generally full rank.
§4.9.1, eq. (4.9.1): sample covariances of the random-phase line-spectrum model converge in mean square, which directly supports consistency of covariance-based frequency estimators.
§4.9.2: every positive Toeplitz covariance matrix has a Carathéodory decomposition R=APA*+σ²I with σ² its minimum eigenvalue and n equal to the complementary multiplicity.

§4.9.3, eqs. (4.9.15)–(4.9.17): under white Gaussian noise, sufficiently separated normalized periodogram ordinates are asymptotically independent χ²(2); the maximum yields a detector with prescribed false-alarm risk α.

§4.9.4, eqs. (4.9.20)–(4.9.23): for an arbitrary real time-varying envelope, NLS frequency estimation reduces to the peak of the DFT of y²(t) over [0,π], because squaring moves envelope energy to a nonzero DC component.

§4.9.5, eqs. (4.9.24)–(4.9.31): cyclic minimization and majorization both monotonically descend the objective, but neither guarantees the global minimum; initialization remains decisive for multimodal NLS.
§4.9.6, eqs. (4.9.68)–(4.9.85): frequency-selective ESPRIT projects FFT-band data off a nuisance subspace, retains rank n when M≥m+n, and recommends m=floor(M/2) to maximize independent equations.

§4.9.7, eqs. (4.9.98)–(4.9.121): a 2D sinusoidal sample array admits a linearly parameterized full-row-rank basis for the left null space of its structured data matrix, enabling 2D extensions of modified MUSIC.
Exercise 4.9, eq. (4.10.8): forward–backward symmetrization cannot worsen the condition number: cond(R)≥cond(R+U*R^TU) for Hermitian R and unitary U.
pedagogy: The two chapters move from a generative model to covariance identities, then to estimators, numerical implementation, failure modes, and exercises. Derivations are proof-forward but consistently tied to signal-processing interpretations: AR coefficients become predictors, reflection coefficients become partial correlations, SVD truncation becomes noise cleaning, and ESPRIT becomes rotational invariance. Boxed algorithms make the main procedures machine-codable. The authors repeatedly compare statistical accuracy, conditioning, complexity, identifiability, and model mismatch rather than presenting formulas in isolation. Complements contain research-level extensions and full proofs; exercises range from short derivations to substantial Monte Carlo labs, algorithm implementation, Doppler radar, and sunspot/lynx data. Prerequisites are graduate-level probability and random processes, DTFT/z-transform methods, linear algebra (eigendecomposition, SVD, projections, LS/TLS), and basic numerical optimization. The source assumes the reader can move comfortably between stochastic models, polynomial roots, structured matrices, and computation.

gems: §3.2, p. 87: rational PSDs are not merely convenient; by Weierstrass they form a dense family for continuous spectra, giving a crisp approximation-theoretic reason for model-based estimation.

§3.4.2, pp. 93–94: the same LS formula becomes either Yule–Walker or covariance LS solely through which boundary rows are included—a concrete illustration of how finite-record conventions change bias and stability.
§3.5, pp. 94–97: narrowband work may test AR orders 50–100; using Toeplitz structure changes the all-orders cost from O(n_max⁴) to O(n_max²), a dramatic algorithmic payoff.
§3.6, pp. 101–103: MA modeling and rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimation are shown to be the same assumption in two languages: covariance lags outside ±m are exactly zero.
§3.7.1, pp. 104–105: higher covariance lags are useful only while their slowly decaying signal component dominates estimation noise; this gives an intuitive rule for when overdetermination helps.
§3.7.2, pp. 107–108: the two-stage ARMA method estimates an unobserved innovation by first pretending the process is a high-order AR model—a memorable latent-variable bootstrap.

§3.8.1, pp. 111–113: an infinite family of state-space triples produces the same transfer function via similarity transforms; subspace estimation succeeds by choosing one well-conditioned representative rather than forcing a canonical form.
§3.9.2, pp. 118–119: every next valid covariance lies inside a literal disk in the complex plane, and selecting the center at each step produces the maximum-entropy extension.
§3.9.3, pp. 119–122: Burg turns a multidimensional AR fit into scalar reflection-coefficient updates and proves stability from the elementary inequality 2|c*d|≤c*c+d*d.
§3.9.5, pp. 125–129: the chapter explicitly frames negative PSD repair as ‘factoring the unfactorable,’ then replaces a nonlinear quartic MA fit by convex covariance fitting.
Exercise C3.18, pp. 139–140: two sinusoids at 0.24π and 0.26π with N=64 form a compact super-resolution stress test that exposes resolution, spurious lines, order sensitivity, and pole/zero behavior.
§4.1, pp. 146–147: a line spectrum’s impulses have zero support and finite area 2πα_k²; drawing them as ordinary finite-height peaks obscures the key distinction.

§4.1, p. 148: the authors call the periodogram comparison ‘unfair’ because parametric super-resolution spends exact model information; this is an excellent antidote to magical interpretations of resolution.
§4.3, p. 152: with N=300 and SNR=30 dB, the asymptotic NLS frequency error is about 10⁻⁵, comparable to roundoff in a 32-bit fixed-point processor.

§4.3, pp. 153–155: the maximum of the ordinary periodogram is exactly the NLS solution for one complex sinusoid, and its largest n peaks are principled initializers when lines are separated by more than 2π/N.
§4.4, pp. 157–159: SVD rank truncation is both numerical regularization and statistical ‘noise cleaning’; the same prior rank knowledge solves two problems at once.
§4.5, pp. 161–162: MUSIC’s pseudospectrum is explicitly not a PSD, while Pisarenko is simply the smallest legal MUSIC problem m=n+1—two clarifications often lost in abbreviated treatments.
§4.7, p. 167: ESPRIT avoids pseudospectrum searches and signal/noise root sorting; the authors recommend it as the first choice because its eigenvalues directly carry frequency phases.
§4.8, p. 170: making a covariance estimate fully Toeplitz can destroy exact noiseless finite-sample rank, so enforcing more visible structure can paradoxically make the estimate worse.
§4.9.3, pp. 174–177: an erratic periodogram becomes a formal detector by normalizing its Fourier-grid ordinates, using their χ²(2) law, and thresholding the maximum at a chosen false-alarm risk.

§4.9.4, pp. 177–179: when the amplitude envelope averages to zero, the ordinary DFT has a valley at the carrier; squaring the samples gives the envelope a DC component and creates a peak at twice the carrier.
Exercise 4.1, pp. 198–199: monostatic Doppler radar reduces speed measurement to frequency estimation through ω_D=2ωv/c, directly connecting abstract line spectra to a physical instrument.

Exercises C3.20 and C4.14, pp. 142–143 and 206: the same sunspot and lynx records are revisited with nonparametric, AR/ARMA, and line-spectrum tools, encouraging triangulation rather than allegiance to one estimator.
